title: Hybrid provisioner and fair-queueing for tenant-preserving embedding throughput
creator: Marisol Gomez
description: Problem: Embedding endpoints are seeing uneven tail latencies and tenant head-of-line blocking during short bursts. Current autoscalers respond at pool level which leads to noisy neighbor effects and expensive overprovisioning for bursty tenants. Goal: Implement a hybrid provisioning and fair-queueing layer that preserves per-tenant throughput SLOs, reduces median and tail queue time, and lowers steady-state cost by avoiding conservative pool-wide headroom allocations.
background: Recently multiple production incidents surfaced where a few tenants issued large embedding floods (many short requests) and caused elevated queue times for others. Existing mitigations (warm pools and simple rate-limits) either still allow transient unfairness or require large warm-pool reserves that increase cost. We need a design that balances fairness, latency SLOs, and cost per embedding.
technical_design: Overview: Introduce a hybrid provisioner that combines lightweight per-tenant soft reservations with a global elastic pool and a fair-queueing admission controller. Key components: 1) Soft reservations: allocate small, quick-to-grant token buckets per tenant based on historical baseline QPS and recent trend scores. These tokens buy short bursts without touching global scaling. 2) Fair queueing: implement deficit round robin (DRR)-style scheduler at the router that serves tenant requests in weighted round-robin segments, with weight derived from SLA tier and recent consumption. 3) Predictive headroom signal: use 5m and 1h moving-average anomaly detectors (existing telemetry) to pre-warm pool capacity when an upswing is predicted. 4) Elastic global pool: autoscaler remains but with reduced hysteresis because per-tenant soft reservations absorb microbursts. 5) Backpressure and slow-fail: when both token buckets and pool capacity are exhausted, respond with well-typed 429 with Retry-After and optional queued-wait tokens for long-running callers. Compatibility: design integrates with current routing and tenant accounting; uses the same KV cache and model shard pinning as existing serving runtime. Implementation notes: implement scheduler as a small Go service in front of the embedding workers to minimize changes to runtime, use Redis for short-lived token buckets with strict TTLs, and reuse existing autoscaler metrics endpoint for predictive signal input.
tradeoffs: Pros: reduces tail queue time for non-bursting tenants, avoids large warm-pool sizes, enables per-tenant fairness and SLA differentiation. Cons: adds scheduler complexity and a small amount of extra state (tokens), potential for slight increase in median latency for very high-priority tenants under extreme global saturation, increased operational surface (new telemetry and dashboards). Alternative of strict per-tenant hard reservations rejected because it would significantly increase cost and reduce utilization efficiency.
acceptance_criteria: P99 embedding queue wait time reduced by >=40% for baseline tenants under mixed workload tests
No single tenant surge causes >2x increase in other tenants' P95 queue time in synthetic multi-tenant stress tests
End-to-end median embedding latency improves or stays within 5% of current for non-burst traffic
Autoscaler triggers less frequently for transient bursts (measured as >30% fewer scale events for 1-2 minute spikes in traffic tests)
Documentation and runbook published (Confluence) and on-call trained
rollout_plan: 1) Lab run: unit + integration tests against synthetic traffic generator (1 week). 2) Canary: enable for a small set of low-risk tenants with observability flags and increase gradually over 48 hours. 3) Tiered rollout: opt-in for customers in Developer tier, then move to default for Standard after 2 weeks of stable telemetry. 4) Full rollout gating: must pass load tests and have no regressions in cost-per-embedding and error rates. Rollback: feature flag to disable scheduler and fall back to existing router; immediate rollback if error rate or tail latency regress beyond thresholds.
tasks: Scheduler prototype (Go) and Redis token-bucket integration
Router changes to add DRR-based admission controller
Predictive signal pipeline hookup to autoscaler pre-warm hook
End-to-end integration tests with synthetic multi-tenant load generator
Dashboard (Console) tiles for per-tenant queue wait and token exhaustion
progress_updates: 2026-02-20: Kickoff meeting with product, infra, and on-call. Agreed on hybrid approach and KPIs. Action: Daniel to draft design doc.
2026-02-24: Design doc posted: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Hybrid+Provisioner+Design. Feedback from SRE to prefer Redis cluster with TTL over in-memory tokens for survivability.
2026-03-02: Prototype scheduler implemented (internal branch) and basic DRR validated locally. GitHub PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/1453

2026-03-08: Integration test shows 45% reduction in P99 queue time for baseline tenants in synthetic mixed workload (details in test dashboard). Need to tune token bucket sizing to avoid starving bursty premium tenants.
2026-03-12: Canary gating checklist prepared. Feature flag path implemented. Planning canary for 3 dev tenants next week.
risks: 1) Token buckets could be gamed by malicious tenants (mitigate with rate-limits and fraud detection). 2) Scheduler adds another failure domain—ensure graceful fallback to existing router and health checks. 3) Incorrect weight calculation could unfairly penalize some tenants—need conservative default weights and emergency admin override.
tests: Synthetic multi-tenant stress harness with configurable burst patterns
Chaos tests: simulate Redis token store latency and validate graceful degradation
Load tests measuring scale events with/without predictive headroom enabled
Backward compatibility tests for embedding client SDKs and existing retry behavior
Cost regression tests to ensure no >10% increase in cost_per_1k_embeddings after rollout
